Newly emerged chicks weigh approximately 26.4 grams [Wwb = approximately 26.4 grams], a relatively modest neonatal mass that reflects the semi-precocial developmental strategy of this species. This initial body mass is notably low compared to the ultimate adult wet weight, which field surveys of breeding colonies in Southern California have consistently recorded at 241.7 grams [Wwi = 241.7 grams]. The roughly nine-fold increase in body mass from hatching to adulthood underscores the rapid growth trajectory that nestling terns must sustain during their brief period of parental dependence. Comparative data from related taxa suggest that this growth rate is typical for inshore-foraging terns that exploit abundant, seasonally predictable prey such as anchovy and sardine, which provide the high-protein diet necessary for such accelerated mass accumulation.

This relatively short nestling period is slightly shorter than that of the larger Caspian tern but aligns well with values reported for the closely related Sandwich tern. The timing of fledging is critically linked to the peak availability of small epipelagic fish in the coastal waters adjoining the colony, as newly fledged juveniles remain dependent on parental provisioning for several weeks after nest departure. This synchrony between developmental timing and resource pulses is a hallmark of the breeding strategy of Thalasseus elegans and is thought to have been shaped by the predictable oceanographic conditions of its primary breeding range.

First reproduction, corresponding to the laying of the first clutch, typically occurs at 2 years after hatching [tR = 2 years after hatching] at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. The gap between sexual maturity and the commencement of reproductive effort is common among long-lived seabirds and is generally interpreted as a period during which young birds refine their foraging skills, establish pair bonds, and acquire a nesting territory. Delaying reproduction allows individuals to attain the body condition and experience necessary to maximize the success of their first breeding attempt.

The reproductive biology of Thalasseus elegans is thus characterized by a conservative, K-selected strategy in which parental care is intensive, chick growth is rapid but energetically costly, and the probability of success for any given nesting attempt is maximized through a combination of single-egg clutches and extended biparental provisioning. Such low annual reproductive output places a premium on adult survival and longevity.
